hook.line: In a hard conversation, "I can't" and "I won't" are very different things, and people hear the difference. Spanish gives you two small tools to say exactly which one you mean. Tomás needs both when Altamira's offer arrives.

examples.es: No soy capaz de decirle que no.
examples.en: I can't bring myself to say no to him.
I'm willing to negotiate. (a man speaking)
I'm willing to give in. (a woman speaking)
Are you willing to listen? (to a man)

examples.es: ¿Estaría dispuesto a que lo revisemos juntos?
examples.en: Would you be willing for us to go over it together? (formal, to a man)
We are capable of fixing this.

rule:
Two pairs, each with its own little word:

*ser capaz de* + infinitive: you have what it takes, or you can't bring yourself to. Use *soy*, *eres*, *somos*, and *capaz* becomes *capaces* for several people.

*estar dispuesto a* + infinitive: you are willing, a state of mind. Use *estoy*, *estás*, and *dispuesto* becomes *dispuesta* for a woman, *dispuestos* for several.

Don't swap the little words: *de* with *capaz*, *a* with *dispuesto*.

To ask someone to agree to a plan, add *que* and "imagined" verb: *dispuesto a que lo revisemos*.
smallPrint: Teachers call both of these adjective plus preposition constructions. In some parts of Latin America, *capaz que llueva* also means "maybe it will rain", a colloquial use you only need to recognise.

readAndPick.es: No soy capaz de decirle que no.
options: I'm not willing to tell him no.
I can't bring myself to say no to him.
He can't say no to me.
I'm not willing to give in.
We are capable of fixing this.
We are willing to fix this.
I'm willing to listen. (a man speaking)
I'm willing to listen. (a woman speaking)

readAndPick.es: ¿Estaría dispuesto a que lo revisemos juntos?
options: Would you be willing for us to go over it together? (formal)
Would you be able to go over it alone? (formal)

readAndPick.es: Ellos no están dispuestos a negociar.

yourTurn.prompt: Choose *soy* or *estoy*: No ___ capaz de decirle que no. Type the whole sentence.
yourTurn.answer: No soy capaz de decirle que no.
yourTurn.why: *Capaz* goes with *ser*: it is about what you can bring yourself to do.

yourTurn.prompt: Choose *de* or *a*: Estoy dispuesto ___ negociar. Type the whole sentence.
I'm willing to negotiate. (a man speaking)
yourTurn.why: *Estar dispuesto a* says what you are willing to do now.

yourTurn.prompt: I can't bring myself to ask him for forgiveness.
yourTurn.answer: No soy capaz de pedirle perdón.
yourTurn.why: *No soy capaz de* plus the infinitive, with *le* glued on.

yourTurn.prompt: Are you willing to listen? (to a man you call *tú*)
yourTurn.why: *Estás* for *tú*, and *dispuesto* because he is a man.

yourTurn.prompt: Make it a woman speaking: Estoy dispuesto a ceder.
yourTurn.why: The adjective follows the speaker: a woman says *dispuesta*.

yourTurn.prompt: Make it negative: Estoy dispuesto a ceder. Say: I'm not willing to give in. (a man speaking)
yourTurn.why: *No* goes straight in front of the verb.

yourTurn.prompt: Make it about we: We are capable of fixing this.

pitfalls.wrong: No estoy capaz de decirle que no.
pitfalls.right: No soy capaz de decirle que no.
pitfalls.why: Almost. *Capaz* is used with *ser*, while *dispuesto* is used with *estar*.
Being willing is a state of mind right now, so it takes *estar*.

personal: Say one thing you are willing to do and one you can't bring yourself to do: *Estoy dispuesto a…* or *Estoy dispuesta a…*, and *No soy capaz de…*
